I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and in order to do so I will read the following telegram from the secretary of the Grain Growers' Association of Saskatchewan.
Moosejaw, Saak., March 9, 1912. W. E. Knowles, M.P., Ottawa.
Whilst fullest discussion was afforded before Senate committee last year, farmers are fearful that through the influence of elevator and transportation companies at Ottawa farmers' friends will be handicapped and their interests sacrificed. Our association is ready to send delegation if in your opinion their cause may be assisted.
FRED. W. GREEN, Secretary, Saskatchewan G.G.A.,
Moosejaw.
I wish to ask the hon. minister whether he will give me an assurance or an intimation that the progress of the Grain Bill will be delayed for a sufficient length of time to give the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association an opportunity to send this delegation here. I should think it could be here by the end of this week. I understand that the Bill has now been waiting for a week, and I submit that the matter is of sufficient urgency that it might be further delayed till they arrive. I hope the hon. minister can give me that intimation so that I may answer this telegram.
I think my hon. friend may rest assured that the interest of the farmers is perfectly safe in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and of the government.
The farmers do not think so.

The farmers do not all think one way. There are a great many farmers in the Northwest, and I fear that comparatively few of them have been represented here. However, I think it is not necessary to delay the passage of the Grain Bill through this House. If these or any other gentlemen wish to come here, they will have an opportunity of conferring with me or with the leader of the Upper House or with their friends, and if anything is put before the department or the government which they consider to be vital in the matter, a change could be made in the Bill in the Senate just as well as in the House. I would not like at this stage of the session to delay the third reading of the Bill in this House.
House in committee on Bill (No. 68) respecting the Queen's College at Kingston, and to change its name to Queen's University at Kingston.-Mr. Nickle.

The last time the Bill was before the Committee of the Whole the bon. member for the St. Lawrence Division, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), moved that the committee now rise, and said:
I do not wish to kill the Bill, but I have endeavoured on three occasions to get the opinion of the Justice Department on this question. My hon. friend from Kingston states that the Private Bills Committee has had that opinion. I am not a member of that committee, and I think we are entitled to have that opinion laid on the table of this House. There are some clauses in the Bill that we have pleaded with the promoters to leave out, because they are insulting to a large number of people. As long as clause 20 remains in the Bill, I will take every chance to defeat it. I stated to the promotor of the Bill that if that clause were struck out. I would not raise the question of jurisdiction.
From the utterances of the hon. gentleman, it is perfectly clear that he admits the general principle of the Bill, but finds fault with certain of its clauses.. Under these circumstances, it seems radically unfair that he should place before the House a motion that the committee now rise, the effect of which would be that the Bill would be killed so far as this House is concerned. Perhaps it would be only fair, as the personnel of the committee to-day is not exactly the same as that of ten days' ago, that I should outline briefly the history of this legislation and the position of its promoters with regard to it. As I stated on a previous occasion, Queen's University was incorporated in 1841 by royal charter, and the preamble is as follows-
151i
Whereas the establishment of a college within the province of Upper Canada, in North America, in connection with the Church of Scotland, for the education of youth in the principles of the Christian religion; and for their instruction in the various branches of science and literature, would greatly conduce to the welfare of our said province.
Provision is made in the cnarter that the university shall be managed by 27 trustees, 15 of whom shall be laymen in full connection with the church of Scotland, and 12 shall be ministers of the Presbyterian church, the Principal of the university to be a minister of the Presbyterian church. On the occasion of the union of the Free church with the bid church of Scotland in Canada, legislation was sought in the Ontario legislature and also in this parliament, with the result that the control of the university was then vested in 27 trustees, who were given authority to elect their successors when a vacancy occurred on the board.
The whole spirit of Queen's from its inception has been against religious intolerance. It was founded as a protest against the restriction of King's College,. Toronto, now Toronto university, where a student was bound to take a test oath before he could have the advantage of that institution. At no time has Queen's required a student to take a test oath. In 1902 the late Rev. G. M. Grant, then Principal of the university, had before the General Assembly of Canada, a measure for the cutting away from Queen's of her Presbyterian control, and in 1903 a Bill was introduced in parliament to that effect. Unfortunately the reverend gentleman died shortly after the Bill was introduced, and from 1903 until 1911 nothing was done in regard to the subject. However in 1911 the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church in Canada consented to the university becoming separated from the Presbyterian church, but laid down as a condition precedent to that separation, that the distinctively Christian character of the university should be maintained, and at that time appointed two committees, one/ of which was to co-operate with the trustees of the university in securing legislation, the other to watch the interests of the theological faculty. In the Bill of 1903, as presented by the late Principal Grant, clause No. 26 was identical with clause 20 as it appears in the present Bill, but in the Bill of 1910, as originally drafted by the trustees, the words:
-save the profession of Christianity.
as they now appear in clause 20 of the present Bill, were omitted. When the two committees of the Presbyterian church and the committee of the university came together to confer on the terms of this Bill,.

those who had the responsibility of protecting the rights of the Theological Faculty of the Presbyterian church objected to clause 20 standing as it was then drawn, and insisted that the words,
*	save the profession of Christianity,' be introduced. The Presbyterian church, as I outlined a moment ago, gave consent to this separation on certain terms, and, bowing to the judgment of the Theological Committee of the Presbyterian church, the trustees and the co-operating committee of the ehurch agreed to these words being reinstated, and it is in that way that the words now appear in the Bill. Perhaps it is only fair that I should place before the House my views on this question, because the Bill, as I have already pointed out, is private legislation. It is not a Bill for which I am primarily responsible. The Bill that I introduced in this House relates to an institution that is domiciled in Kingston. I might say that my personal views are that the incorporation of the words
*	save the profession of Christianity,' is a mistake from the point of view of the university and from the point of view of the church. It is a mistake because, in my Judgment, it will cut off the university from taking advantage of the intellect of certain of the Jewish people who display great aptitude in matters, legal, literary, and scientific. It will be a stumbling block in the way of the university when application is made to the government of Ontario for assistance, because the government may then feel justified in saying: ' You are not national in spirit because your restrictions exclude from your trustee board and professional chairs, certain representative Canadian citizens. I think also it is a retrograde movement, because is puts restrictions on Queen's that are not now there, and furthermore, I doubt if the movement is one in the right direction. But, Sir, there is another question that I have to consider, and it is one that has caused me great worry and anxiety. The question is this: How far am I justified in setting up my views as against the views contained in this Bill, which represent the wisdom of the Presbyterian church and the wisdom of the trustee board of Queen's university? The only ground on which I would be justified as a member of parliament, in voting against this Bill, is that within its four corners are inconsistencies and improprieties from a national point of view. I have listened to the arguments advanced by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike), and of those whom he contends he primarily represents, and I have been struck with the fact that only on one ground can he hope to succeed in having either clause 3 or clause 20 amended or altered in any way. If I interpret correctly the argument of the

member for St. Lawrence, it is that there is an inconsistency in having in the Bill clauses 3 and 20. If the members of the House will follow me they will see that clause 3 of Bill (No. 68) reads as follows :
The management and discipline of the university shall he in every_ respect freed from all denominational restrictions, and it shall be national and non-denominational in its character and management;
Clause 20 is to the following effect:
The university shall continue distinctively Christian, but no religious test or qualification save the profession of Christianity shall be required of or appointed for any officer, trustee, member of council, or official of the university. Laymen shall be eligible to any position therein.
The argument of the hon. member for St. Lawrence is that there is an inconsistency in the Bill in saying that a university shall be national, and at the same time saying that it shall be distinctly Christian. The promoters of this Bill answer those objections by referring to cases decided in the courts in England and in Ontario. In the case of the Crown versus Milburn, which is reported in the Law Beports, Exchequer Court Cases, 1867, volume 2, page 230 (234) Baron Kelly enunciated the doctrine that ' Christianity is part and parcel of the law of the land.'
They also draw my attention to a case that was decided in Ontario, in 1879, Pringle versus Napanee, in which the Divisional Court held that Christianity in general and not simply the tenets of a particular sect is part of the recognized law of the province.
In Shirley's Leading Cases, fifth edition, at page 155 to 158, the same principle is enunciated: that Christianity is part of the common law of England. The argument might be advanced that while Christianity was part of the law of England, yet parliament with plenary jurisdiction could vary in any way the desire to enact a law of this sort. But then the promoters of the Bill estop me still further by drawing my attention to ' Hansard ' of 1896, page 5623, in which the late Minister of Justice spoke as follows when the Lord's Day Act was before this House for discussion:
The general scope of this Bill is indicated by its title, an Act respecting the Lord's Day, an Act intended to secure the better observance of the Christian Sunday, throughout the whole of Canada. Christianity, I need scarcely say, is recognized as constituting part of the law of Canada, as it is of the law of the British Empire, and statutes declaring certain things to he offences because they profane the sanctity of the Chritian Sabbath have been frequent upon the statute books of the imperial parliament and of this parliament and of its predecessors.

As a member of parliament, in the face of such decisions and of the statements of the late Minister of Justice is it correct t-o say that Christianity is not a part of the law of this land, and that a Bill is inconsistent which states in one clause that a university shall' be National and in another that it shall be distinctly Christian? After giving the matter the mosit careful consideration that I have been able, I have come to the conclusion that there is nothing necessarily inharmonious in this Bill. To say that a university is National and to say that a university is distinctly Christian, is practically saying legally one and the same thing, but in different terms. I might say for the enlightenment of my hon. friend (Mr. Bick-erdike) that when this clause was drafted it was never thought for one moment that it would be offensive to the Hebrew citizens of this country.
Queen's is at all times willing to open her doors to men of other faiths, and I trust the time will never come when Queen's will feel that she need shut her doors in the face of any man who comes seeking for instruction. This university was founded by the Presbyterian Church and has been endowed with Presbyterian money; and it would seem that these people are within the sphere of their right when they ask this parliament to ratify legislation that widens the scope of her operations. Some people might object that a clear severance should be made between education and the state; and, I think, when they try to put on the term ' National ' as used a narrow meaning, and say that because the university is declared to be a National university, therefore it becomes the ward, so to speak of the state, they do not give to the word its true and direct meaning. The idea that the trustees had in the use of that word was that ' National ' meant that Queen's is a free institution to which every student could freely come, that it was geographically National; and, while certain restrictions were put on the staff, and on the trustee board, she was National in this, that she offered free opportunity to those who seek an education, who desire to take advantage of the opportunities she possesses. And I think that when my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, Montreal, (Mr. Bick-erdike), considers the matter he will see the propriety of allowing the preamble of this Bill to pass, and that we should discuss in committee the modifications he desires, when it may be possible, that some solution of a very vexed question may be reached. It would be radically unfair that because certain terms are objectionable to him, and to those whom he purports to represent the whole Bill should be killed. The principle of the Bill was settled on its second reading, and it is not unfair to ask
that the committee pass the preamble, and proceed to the consideration of the various clauses.
On section 3,
3. The management and discipline of the university shall he in every respect freed from all denominational restrictions, and it shall be national and undenominational in its character and management.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the excuses given by my hon. friend (Mr. Nickle), for being the champion of the persecutors of the Jews to-day, and I am sorry he did not make a better hand at it. I am pleased to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), in his place, because I intend to raise again the question of jurisdiction. The Bill came before this House, and had its first and second reading with clause 2 in it stating1 ' the university is hereby declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.' But at the request of the promoters of the Bill, that clause was withdrawn so that the Bill no longer stands as declaring the university to be for the general advantage of Canada. Well, if it is not for the general advantage of Canada, this becojnes merely an educational Bill; and I would ask on what ground this parliament of Canada is asked to deal with it. I submit respectfully that this Bill should be referred to the Department of Justice, as there is a question of doubt, and a very-grave doubt, whether this House has jurisdiction to deal with it or not. The very-fact that the Ontario authorities sent a representative to the committee to enter a protest against this House taking up this Bill, against our usurping their jurisdiction in educational matters, is surely a reason why we should pause before going on with this measure. Though the clause, has been eliminated declaring it a work? for the general advantage of Canada, yet we have section 3 declaring that the university shall be * National and undenominational.'
If it is undenominational, then section 20 is a direct contradiction. As to the question of jurisdiction, a man does not need to be a lawyer to understand the British North America Act on this subject. That Act states distinctly and defines exactly what this parliament can do, and what the legislatures of the provinces can do. This House has no more constitutional right to deal with an educational matter than the legislatures of Ontario or Quebec would have to gTant a bank charter. So, I move that we do not proceed further with the consideration of the Bill, but that the Bill be referred to the Department of Justice to get their opinion as tf>
whether we have or have not jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The motion is not in order in that form. I think the hon. member (Mr. Bickerdike) had better move to report progress. .

Yes, the suggestion
is that progress should be reported for the purpose of referring the matter to the Department of Justice. I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) labours, to some extent at all events, under a misapprehension, when he sets forth the view that the proper method of determining whether this Bill is constitutional or not, and whether this House should proceed to deal with it or not on the question of its constitutionality, is to refer the matter to the Department of Justice-as I understand him, for deoision. I understand that the Minister of Justice and the Department of Justice are not the advisers of this House. As I understand it. the Minister of Justice is the adviser of the Crown and the different departments of government; but I do not understand that it is part of his functions to advise this House, still less do I understand that he has any privilege, or prerogative, or power, to decide for this House whether or no it shall proceed to pass certain legislation upon the consideration of its constitutionality. I think the question of constitutionality of a particular piece of legislation submitted to this House is to toe determined by the House like any other question that arises in connection with the proposed measure. And yet, while all that is perfectly true in my judgment, I, of course, am quite willing to put myself at the service of any member of this House who thinks my opinion upon a question may be useful to him; but I wish to point out that any opinion I express would be only the opinion of a member of this (House, and would be entitled to such weight only as might properly belong to my personal opinion.
We will abide by It.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is true, the private Bills committee did send this Bill to the department, submitting to it this question of constitutionality, and one of the officers of the department did wait upon the committee and express to them, in the first place, the view I have just set forth, that it was not, perhaps, the proper function of the department to advise the committee, but, nevertheless the department, like its head, was at the service of this House or of any committee of this House that might consider that its opinion could be useful. Now, with Tegard to the question of the constitutionality of legislation concerning Mr. BICKERDIKE.
education, and more particularly concerning this particular educational corporation, I think it is well that we should bear in mind that we are not approaching a perfectly new question. We should have present to our minds the fact that this House has already three times assumed jurisdiction over this particular corporation, and acted on the assumption that it had jurisdiction to enact legislation with regard to this university. Now that creates a situation where, no doubt, things have been done in virtue of that legislation, very possibly, and very probably rights have been acquired under that legislation. I think that in that condition of affairs it behoves us to be very careful indeed before we undertake to pronounce, as we would impliedly pronounce by rejecting this legislation purely on the ground that we have no constitutional power to deal with the matter, that the previous legislation was unconstitutional. As I have said, that legislation has been enacted and rights have been created under it, and that being true, I think we must recognize that it is much more proper that the question of the constitutionality of that legislation should be left to be determined by the courts, than that we should take it upon ourselves, by saying now that on this new legislation we have no jurisdiction whatever, practically to declare that the previous legislation was unconstitutional.

But I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that legislation similar to that of Bill (No. 68) has never been before this House; the three times that he refers to were on an entirely different Bill. Bill (No. 69) at present is the theological Bill. Bill (No. 68) is purely an educational Bill, a Bill the like of which has never been before this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman does not deny that there has been before this House legislation with respect to Queen's College at Kingston.
That was the theological college.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Whether it was or was not, the purpose of this Bill is to modify that particular corporation, that is the corporation concerning which we are asked to legislate. I think the fact itself that parliament has already assumed jurisdiction with regard to this corporation to legislate on three different occasions, is sufficient reason why this House should deal with the Bill upon its merits, and determine whether or not, looking at it from the point of the merits or demerits of its provisions, they should pass it or not. After all, it is private legislation, and the parties promoting this Bill are those who will run the greatest and most serious risks if it should be passed and be subsequently determined to be unconstitutional. I think it is fair

for us to assume that they have been advised upon that question. That being so, if it be my proper function to advise this House, as far as any member may be disposed to ask for my advice, I would suggest that the Bill be allowed to pass upon a consideration of its merits or demerits, without regard to the constitutional question. I may say that the same matter was brought up in connection with the legislation of 1889 and on that .occasion Sir John Thompson, 1 think, expressed substantially the view that I have now submitted upon the question of the constitutionality of the legislation. I do not think it would be proper for this House to go back to the position as it stood before that legislation, and undertake now to treat the question of our jurisdiction over this situation just as if that legislation had never taken place. That being so, I think it would be unfair that we should put on record an opinion that might even throw doubt upon the validity of the legislation which has been enacted in the past. For my part, I would be disposed to think that the proper line of action for this House to take would be to deal with the Bill upon its merits, and I would not at all accept the position, if it were thrown upon me, of expressing an opinion which in any sense this House should accept as decisive in determining this question under the present circumstances.

Under the circumstances, I will withdraw my motion, I always take the advice of the Minister of Justice in this House, on whichever side of the House he may be sitting. I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to clause 3. I think he will agree with me this time that that clause is in contradiction with clause 20.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see that there is any question of law involved in section 3. I think it is a section that any layman is just as competent to deal with as a lawyer; therefore, I do not see that there is any reason why the Minister of Justice should be called upon to express an opinion. But if I were to express an opinion, I would say, speaking only_ for myself, I think that it is very undesirable that we should attach the name ' National ' to any institution that is going to be governed, controlled and directed by any private individuals, or any corporation of the nature of this one. Without going into the consideration of the question whether there be or be not anything inconsistent in the terms of section 3 with those of section 20, I think the word ' National ' as applied to an institution of this kind is very undesirable, because the word ' National ' is susceptible of more than one meaning. The word ' National ' may properly be attributed to an institution of any kind that was
under the control and direction of the nation, or an institution which the nation chose to select and dignify, and set forth as its conception of what a national institution ought to be.
I do not want to say a word derogatory to this very great institution and to the great work it has done and is doing, and of course we must all join in approval of its aspirations to give to that work in the future a National character in the sense of making of it an institution open to the whole nation and conducted from the point of view of conducing most effectively to the spread of education throughout the whole nation. But while I feel that way about it, I do not think we should by an Act of parliament attach this designation of ' National ' to the institution. I quite understand that the promoters of the Bill do not intend to have that designation attached to it as conveying any idea of connection between the institution and the nation, and I fully sympathize with their desire to affirm that their purpose is to carry on an institution which shall enure to the benefit of the whole nation, and to carry it on upon lines that will make it acceptable to the whole nation. But that is the sentiment that inspired those who control all of our great educational bodies; there are other great universities in this country whose motive and desire is to prove these institutions of National use and benefit, and I am sure the gentlemen of Queen's themselves would admit this desire to be quite as sincere as their own. That being so, if we enact in this parliament a declaration that this university shall be National in its character, then there is no reason why we should not enact the same thing for every one of these universities, and if this epithet or description is to be common to all universities it ceases to have any distinguishing meaning at all. Thus no matter how anxious we may be to recognize this desire of Queen's University to be so described at least from the point of view of being an institution desirous of doing good work for the nation, I sympathize with the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) that the word ' National ' should not appear in this description of the university or of its proposed character and management as set forth in clause 3.
What would you use?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I ,think we require nothing beyond what is in the clause:
The management and discipline of the university shall be in every respect freed from all denominational restrictions.

As I understand the difficulty lies here. Under the charter the university was particularly and peculiarly limited to the provinces of Ontario and

Quebec, Upper and Lower Canada. The promoters wish to incorporate in the Bill some expression that will clearly convey to the people of Canada that that restriction has been deleted and that the university is now as wide as the bounds of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is it contemplated that the operations of the university should be carried on in more than one province?

At present it draws students from every province in Canada and in fact from all over the world. The idea they want to impress on the people is that the university has ceased to be provincial in respect to Upper and Lower Canada and has taken on itself a wider and more significant prospect.

If I understood the Minister of Justice his idea is that all of this section after the word * restrictions ' should be omitted. That would appear to_ me to be more correct legislation. Admitted that this parliament has power to deal with this Bill in common with the rights of the local legislature, it would be wiser if such legislation were referred to the provincial legislatures. I do not quite understand the purport of this Bill. I have got an impression from some source that this legislation has in view a participation in a fund established by a philanthropist the restrictions of which are that no educational institution controlled by any denomination shall participate in the benefit of that fund. It may be that this particular Bill has no relation to that fund, but I know that some universities in Canada have sought to free themselves from denominational influences with a view to securing the monetary advantages which would accrue by reason of such freedom. It would be improper for us to continue in this Bill the words ' and it shall be National and1 undenominational in its character and management1 if we intend at the same time to enact section 20, which clearly and unequivocally places a religious test upon all those who seek admittance.

The test is applied solely to the management and there is no test in regard to those who seek admittance as students and there never has been from 1841 down to to-day. The test is on the controlling body.
Therefore, it is not undenominational. The moment you require such a test with respect to any officer, professor or president, it ceases to be undenominational.
Oh, no.
I submit that would be the logical result.

I was very careful to look that up. The word ' denominational ' refers to the divisions within the Christian church itself and Queen's is nondenominational in this, that it in no way prevents any person who professes Christianity taking advantage of it. But it is not non-racial; it would prevent a Buddhist or a Japanese. It certainly does place restriction on a number of people. The word ' denominational ' refers only to divisions within the Christian Church.

Section 20 clearly narrows and restricts the terms of section 3. Let us look at the Bill from a broad standpoint. This is a private corporation, religious in a sense, and it has control and management within itself, and they can make any one an officer or a professor. Why should the parliament of Canada be called upon to require that there shall be a religious test with respect to any such officer or professor. It seems to me to be an invidious declaration and one not in harmony with the declaration of the third section of the Bill, and certainly not in harmony with the National aspirations of the university. I am heartily in accord with the remarks of the Minister of Justice and of the hon. member for St. Lawrence Division, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike). It seems to me the third section should be amended by striking out all the words after the word ' restriction,' and that subsequently when we deal, with section 20 we should eliminate all religious tests with respect to the officers or professors. If we give that power to the managing board we enable them to narrow the character of the faculty, and to make it entirely inconsistent with the aims and aspirations set out in the preceding sections of the Bill.
Sections 3 and 20 allowed to stand.
On section 22,

This Bill has been before the law clerk since it passed the Private Bills Committee and he suggested the following amendment as more clearly carrying out the intention of the Bill. I move that section 22 be amended by striking out the first two lines thereof and the following be substituted therefor:
In order to provide for the maintenance of Queen's Theological College, the university shall form an incorporation of said college, and upon its being declared to be a successor of the faculty of theology of Queen's College at Kingston, pay to the said college.

That amendment brings up the question with respect to Bill (No. 69) on the order paper. Whatever reason may be advanced in support of Bill (No. 68) because of previous legislation, no such reason can be given with respect to

Bill (No. 69). It seems to me that Bill (No. 69) is clearly within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature and while, as a matter of expediency, this parliament may be willing to set aside its usual procedure, it should not, without very grave reasons, interfere with the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature in such a matter.
I have opposed the legislation on general principles, with a view to having correct legislation, and with a view to this parliament not interfering in any way with the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. I think you can range over the whole history of the legislation of this character, and you will not find any university or college established in any of the provinces except under the authority of a provincial Act. To seize upon this particular institution, and take it out from all the rest seems to me to be a strange procedure, and I think that as members of this committee we are entitled to have advanced very strong reasons for such a course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It seems to me that whatever consideration applies to the present Bill would apply to the other. Parliament has already legislated twice with regard to this institution, and I suppose that those who are coming to us now for legislation might very well say that inasmuch as that legislation has not been questioned from the time it was enacted by this parliament up to the present, they are justified in coining to us for legislation which manifestly does aiter the status of the university as established by two previous Acts of this parliament. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has submitted considerations on account of which he considers that we are justified in proceeding with this legislation, and it seems to me we shall be equally entitled to deal with the other measure in the same way.

Section agreed to.
On section 3,

With a view to meeting the view's of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), I would suggest that sections 3 and 20 stand over in order that we may try to agree on something that will not be offensive or insulting to any of the minorities in this country and w'ill at the same time carry out the wishes of the university.

I would much prefer to have the word ' National ' struck out
and leave the word ' non-denoininational' in.

The clause would then read as follows:
The management and discipline of the university shall be in every respect free from denominational restrictions.
Would that meet the hon. member's approval ?
It will satisfy me as far as section 3 is concerned.
Will it satisfy you in toto?
I might say, Mr. Chairman, it does not satisfy the hon. member from Kingston.
I have tried to make myself perfectly clear to the House and to the hon. gentleman. I have told him that clause 20 did not meet with my approval-
Then withdraw it.
The hon. gentleman terms me a persecutor of the Jews. I want to again make my position perfectly clear, I am not in favour of that test clause.
Strike it out then.

The hon. gentleman says strike it out. This is Private Bill legislation, which has the ratification of the Presbyterian church and Queen's university, Kingston, and I have no more right to strike that provision out, or to change even a comma, than I have to change the constitution of Canada.
I W'ant to correct the hon. gentleman. When he states this legislation has the endorsation of the Presbyterian church, he is going a little too far. It has nothing of the kind.

This Bill has been endorsed by three committees. First, a committee of Queen's university; second a cooperating committee of the Presbyterian church, nominated by the Moderator at the general assembly held either at Halifax or Ottawa, I forget which; and third, a committee nominated by the Moderator, with the concurrence and sanction of the General Assembly of the church to look after the interests of the Theological Faculty. The Chairman of the first church committee is Dr. Ramsay, of Ottawa. The chairman of the university committee, is Mr. D. B. McLennan, of Cornwall, and the name of the chairman of the third committee, is Dr. Love, of Quebec. These committees were duly appointed, they have placed this Bill in my hands, and they tell me that as member for Kingston, I cannot vary it one jot or tittle. I have told this House, and I have told the

member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) in private conversation, that I do not believe in test oaths. I believe the effect of this Bill will be that the scamp may have access to the professoriate of Queen's university, and the scholar may be excluded. I believe the man who has no principle may say he is a Christian, while the man of integrity, who may happen to be a Jew, will say, that even for the sake of the professorial chair, he will not abandon his religious convictions. When the men who have drafted this Bill tell me that I cannot change one jot or one tittle, I say it is unfair for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) to brand me as a persecutor of the Jews. The Jews of my own constituency know where I _stand in this matter. It is not a question of politics, it is a big question which touches Canada from one end to the other, and which the Presbyterian church feels, touches her to the very foundation. The men who control the destinies of the Presbyterian church maintain that Christianity is the foundation of the common law of this country, and if the issue has been raised, they, as the representatives of that church, insist that that great principle be maintained, that Christianity is part of the common law of Canada, part of the common law of England, and they rely on the enunciation of that principle by the late Minister of Justice. What right have I as a commoner of this House, and as a young lawyer without power and without reputation, to set my judgment up as against the judgment of men who sit on the Bench in England and who occupy the Woolsack in Canada, and have represented this Canada of ours as Ministers of Justice in former parliaments? Why should I be branded as a persecutor of the Jews because I take this stand? It is not fair politics and I resent it. I do not want to read the member for St. Lawrence a lecture, but we have heard1 enough about the east as against the west, about Roman Catholic as against Protestant. Are v/e going to set Jew against Gentile in this country by striking at the very foundation of the Christianity we revere?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall clause 3 be adopted?
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto.) I move that the section be amended by dropping all the words after the word 'restrictions.'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think notice should be given of such an amendment.

When this Bill was being considered in the Private Bills Committee, as has been so very ably and lucidly pointed out by the member for Kingston, representatives of the different bodies composing the Presbyterian Mr. NICKLE.
church, appeared before that committee and presented this measure as the basis of their agreement. In other words the present Bill represents the conclusions come to by the various bodies in the Presbyterian church, and one of the statements made by them was rather than have the measure changed they would prefer to have it withdrawn. Looking at it in that light to my mind it seems a small matter to not allow this institution to be called National and undenominational. Its operations will extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific by the way of extension lectures; it draws its students from the various provinces; and what harm is there in calling it a National institution, I think it would be in the nature of a breach of trust on the part of this parliament to change the provisions of the Bill in any vital way. I hope the Bill will pass in the way in which it has been presented by the representatives of the Presbyterian church. The Presbyterian church and its members are handing over this private property to the nation as a National asset. Why then should we do anything to diminish the rights and privileges which they possess? I do not think we have any right when they are giving that National asset to this country to vary the terms upon which these interests had agreed in the past. In other words it would be a breach of agreement as between these various parties if we vary or change in any way the restrictions and rights which the Bill provides for, and therefore I hope that the Bill will be passed in the condition in which it now is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I move that we proceed to clause 20.

I cannot agree to clause 3 standing unless clause 20 stands also. Both clauses should stand together, seeing that one is a direct contradiction of the other. If these two clauses are allowed to stand we may get a section drafted that will be satisfactory both to the persecuted and to the persecutors. I throw out that suggestion to my good friend the Minister of Justice.
Where is the contradiction between clause 3, as amended, and clause 20?
You say it is not amended, and that it stands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It cannot be amended without notice.

Then assuming that clause 3 stands, clause 20 should stand as well. I still entertain the hope that the Minister of Justice will draft some clause that will satisfy the Jews as well as the university authorities.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that if clause 3 were amended by striking out everything after the word ' restrictions,' the ground of objection to clause 20 disappears?

No, I think still that clause 20 should be amended.
I think that section 20 should be amendL ed. The amending of section 3 does not have the same effect. Even with section 3 amended, there should be an amendment in section 20, unless you wish

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What amendment is suggested in section 20?

To strike out the words ' save the profession of Christianity.' The section would then read:
The university shall continue distinctively Christian, but no religious test or qualification shall be required of or appointed for any officer, trustee, member of council, or official of the university. Laymen shall be eligible to any position therein.
I think that the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), would1 probably agree to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could quite understand the objection to these words in section 20, if we had left section 3 to stand as it was. But now that section 3 has been amended, it simply comes down to a question of whether parliament shall incorporate a Christian university.
You are legalizing a test.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Perhaps I am taking up too much time, but I want to point out that you are making a law that will not allow this university to employ a Jew in any capacity, even as a janitor. Why pass a law declaring that the great Queen's University shall be debarred from employing a Hebrew in any capacity?
If the university wants it that way, what is the objection ?

Let me tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) this: You are a Presbyterian; so am I. The committee of your church say to the university:	We
have a string around your waist, -and we will not cut the string and free you, unless you agree to certain conditions. The university must agree to the conditions. I have told the House frankly that the university as such did not want these words, but that the church, which is the master of the situation, says that unless these words go in you cannot be free. And the university wants freedom.
-Then, I say, take out the words. I will not be dictated to even by the Presbyterian church.

Not many minutes ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) stated that notwithstanding this Bill was arranged jointly by three committees one of which was selected by the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church, it did not represent the Presbyterian church. Yet we have the suggestion that he and two or three of this House should get together and amend this Bill and arrange it to suit their ideas, upon the basis, I assume, that they represent the Presbyterian church.
I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) does not represent the Presbyterian church.

I believe that the expressions of the Minister of Justice represent the opinion of the Presbyterian church much closer than do those of the hon. member for St. Lawrence. I think we should consider this Bill as a far more important matter than the promotion of the political interests of any hon. member of this House, and that this Bill, which is made not with a view to furthering a political purpose, should not be treated by any member in that way. This is a Bill brought in at the request of the Presbyterian church to deal with one of the great educational institutions of this country. And whether we leave in the word * National ' or not, every Canadian must admit that the great Queen's University is national in its scope, its efforts and the work it is doing. We may ask that the word ' National ' be deleted, but we cannot delete the sentiment which prevails regarding this university. We cannot destroy the National influence which the university is having in Canada. We must not forget that this university, ever since its incorporation has been under the control of the Presbyterian church; and if the churoh is willing at this time to broaden it and to have its charter amended

in such a way as to remove it from the direct influence of the Presbyterian church, I think We should readily assent, on the ground that the Presbyterian church has some right to say on what terms the university shall be handed over to an independent body.
What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Steele) mean by saying ' remove it from the direct influence of *the Presbyterian Church '?
It has been under the direct control of the Presbyterian Church; it has been a Presbyterian body
Where is it going now?
It is now being put in the hands of a body that is undenominational.
In which no church will have control?

No one church. A vote was taken of the graduates of this university, and out of 1,562 voting on the question, 1,430 voted in favour of the change. And on the strength of that vote this broad Bill is brought in. I say we must not forget that, that church has had, in the past, full control of it. They are willing that it should be handed over to an undenominational body to be controlled in the future. But because they are willing to do that, I do not know that we should demand that the church should assent to all reference to Christianity being cut out of the Bill.
Will the hon. gentleman excuse me a moment? Is it not the intention to make this an entirely state institution?

No. It is the intention of the churcn, I have no doubt, simply to carry out the practice in the past, that the intention is that the students attending the university shall be under Christian influences, that there shall be no professor of the university who is not a professed Christian, i It is simply the desire of the church that the university shall uphold the great Christian religion, and that it shall not get into the hands of those who are opponents of the Christian religion. The university has been supported largely by the members of the Presbyterian church; they have endowed it in the past; and I think it is a very slight request that they make when they ask that _ the university shall continue distinctively Christian and that every teacher in it shall be a professor of Christianity.

I hope my suggestion will be adopted in the spirit in which Mr. STEELE.	.
it has been offered, otherwise I should strongly oppose the adoption of section 20. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) the other day quoted largely from Sir John Thompson, a man whose memory we all respect. But the hon. gentleman forgot to say that Sir John Thompson was the man who declared that wherever minorities were found they should be treated not only justly but generously. Now, I ask him if it is just or generous to some half a million good, loyal inhabitants of this country, loyal to the Union Jack, to pass section 20 of this Bill, which is an insult to them, and specially to single them out as unworthy to enjoy equal rights with their fellow citizens in Canada. And here we are asked to legalize that insult. I hope this House will never agree to adopt section 20. We should be very careful in this country how we deal with minorities. Although these men are Jews, they have souls just as well as my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, and why should we single them out for unfair treatment? Why, even a negro, much to his credit, can be a professor in Queen's College, while a Jew cannot. A Jew cannot even be a janitor, cannot even be an employee in that institution; and here you are asking us to pass a law that for all time to come will exclude Jews from Queen's University. A Jew may be one of the best educated men in this country, he may have all the qualifications requisite to make an excellent professor, and yet you impose upon him here a test that he cannot take. England, at a former time, made just such unjust distinctions against Jews. My hon. friend has the evidence by him, and he knows that three universities combined to strike out those religious tests. I think that the secret of England's greatness is the fact that she has always dealt justly and generously by minorities. Is Canada going to do any less? Why should Canada pass a law shutting Jews out from any university in this country? Why should Canada pass a law that would prevent a Jew even from sweeping the streets in front of this university? I think it is an outrage, and on reflection I do not think this House will consent to it. I acquiesced in the opinion of the Minister of Justice on the constitutional question, because he was the Minister of Justice, and believed he was right, although I think he was wrong. I have always taken the ground that educational matters belong exclusively to provincial jurisdiction. Why should this Bill undertake to say that we have jurisdiction here under the British North America Act? I think I have heard my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) argue several times that educational matters belong specially to the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. For my part, I am strongly opposed to section 20,

and I move in amendment to strike out these words ' save the profession of Christianity.' I want to strike out this religious test, and I appeal to hon. members of this House to assist me. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) suggested that a man who wants to become a professor could easily profess the doctrine of Christianity; he said that some men might do so, but he did not think the Jews would, I suppose he meant that they could not. What harm will it do to strike out these words, which are an insult to a large number of loyal Canadians? I see no necessity for them whatever. The hon. member for Kingston himself admits that it would be right to strike them out, but he does not wish to do so because the university authorities wish them to remain in. I think, however, that we should follow our own judgment and strike out these words.

I do not, as a rule,
agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence Division, Montreal '(Mr. Bickerdike), but on this occasion I am obliged to agree with him. It seems to me this amendment he has offered ought to be adopted by this committee. I cannot approach this matter without reminding myself that this House might properly be called Caesar's court. We have no business, as I understand our constitution, to make any distinction between one man and another on the ground of his religion. We are called upon in parliament to legislate only for the welfare of loyal British subjects, and I cannot understand why we should indirectly insult a man who is a good, loyal British subject, as this Bill would do without this amendment. On the other hand, I cannot understand why we should put a premium upon any man joining the Christian religion. I do not think Christianity would be served by exercising any such compulsory powers. This is coercion, and this House ought not to exercise coercion on anybody, no matter to what church or sect he may belong, so long as he is a loyal subject to King George. We are here asked to give sanction to this legislation. We must do it either because the institution is denominational or because it is national. If this is a denominational institution, which has certain rights as such, that is one thing; but to say here that we are going to exclude by Act of parliament, or to sanction the exclusion of certain people from this university because they are not Christians, it seems to me is striking a blow at their citizenship which we ought not to do. Let me remind this House that an atheist, who is further removed from Christianity than a Jew, is perfectly competent to sit in this House, he is just as competent to exercise the franchise as a Christian or anybody else. He has all
rights co-equal with any one of us, whether we are Jews or Christians. Why, Sir, under our constitution the Prime Minister of this country might be an atheist, and competent to advise His Excellency on all matters, and an atheist is even further removed from Christianity than a Jew. We cannot forget that a former Prime Minister of Great Britain Benjamin Disraeli, who became Lord Beaconsfield, was a Jew. I personally feel that I ought not to give a silent vote on this matter or allow the measure to pass without some such amendment as that moved by the hon. member (Mr. Bickerdike). To properly- represent my constituency I must declare for full rights of citizenship for every one without putting any impediment in the way of any citizen, without any attempt to restrict his liberties either by persuasion or coercion in any legislation and I cannot vote that any institution wanting state legislation should be allowed to pick or choose between Jew and Christian.

The last speaker (Mr. Lancaster) and also the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) are apparently arguing on the assumption that this is public legislation; on the contrary it is private legislation, asked by private individuals. I agree with the hon. member for Lincoln that we should not place a bann upon any one by any public legislation, but we have here certain private individuals asking us to pass an Act that is private legislation. They ask for this legislation which is the result of an agreement. The amendment proposed would destroy 'that agreement among the parties. We would be guilty of breach of faith if we accepted this amendment.

Where is the difference in our function? It matters not whether it be a public or a private Bill, parliament is asked to sanction this. If we adopt it we advise His Royal Highness the Governor General to approve a certain Act of parliament and I see no difference in regard to our function between a public and a private Bill. For my part I cannot advise His Royal Highness to sanction any such Bill as this.

As I shall be called upon to vote on this amendment, I do not wish to give a silent vote and shall explain briefly why I propose to support the amendment of the hon. member for St. Lawrence division (Mr. Bickerdike). I am of opinion first that this legislation should come under the provincial legislature, that section 93 of the British North America Act without doubt places educational matters under the legislatures, and that is tne -reason why 1 do not see that this

educational Act should be asked from this parliament. But there is another and a graver reason. The-hon. member for St. Lawrence is perfectly right in saying that this is offering an insult to a religious sect in this country. The Jews are very, very respectable people and as was pointed out a moment ago by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) Benjamin Disraeli, one of the ablest men in the history of Great Britain, -belonged to the Jewish faith. I know from experience that McGill, one of the greatest universities in Canada, does not exclude any man of any faith from a chair in that university. I know that the Minister of Justice, who does not profess the Presbyterian faith with which McGill is very closely allied, occupied for a great many years a professor's chair in that university, in fact I had the honour to be a student of the university when the minister was giving a course of lectures. I speak in favour of the Jews being recognized in this country not from any political point of view, because, to the best of my knowledge, I have not a Jewish voter in Wright. I think if we are going to lay it down as a principle in this country that there shall be no coercion, the Presbyterians should not ask us to sanction an Act which will involve coercion of the Jews, any more than the members of any other faith should ask us to coerce, for instance, the province of Manitoba.
I hardly think it can be argued in this House, that any particular religious body can ask the Canadian parliament to establish any set rule in the educational system, we will say again, in the province of Manitoba, which would exclude either Protestants or Roman Catholics. If we are not going to recognize any established church in this country, and if the universities we charter are to be undenominational, why should not Jews, who believe in God, be recognized just as well as any other religious body? I am very sorry to have to take part in a discussion which does not concern the religious family to which I belong, but since it becomes my duty to vote on this measure, I want to say that I recognize no established church in Canada, and I cannot vote to insult a most respectable element in our community, namely the Jews.

I generally like to agree with my friends, but I must say that I believe a word should be said on behalf of the Presbyterian church in connection with this matter. I happen to be an adherent of that church, and I must protest most strongly against the idea that the Presbyterian church, in connection with this university, has any intention of insulting anybody or doing anything to interfere with Mr. DEVLIN.
anybody's religion. If there is one religious body in the world, against whom that charge cannot be successfully maintained, it is the Presbyterian body, for, if the Presbyterian church has ever stood for anything in this world, it is for toleration, and for education. I am absolutely unable to appreciate the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike), when- he suggests that the legislation before the House is an insult, or is intended to be an insult to any section of the people of Canada. I protest against such an assertion. There is no such intention on the face of the legislation and there is no such intention behind the legislation, in any way, shape or manner. I am not responsible for the legislation in any way, but I cannot sit silent and hear such suggestions mad'e in this House. My understanding of the matter is that the adherents of the Presbyterian church have at stupendous cost and sacrifice to themselves established an educational institution known as Queen's University, which has done great work in the cause of education, and, if you like, in the cause of Christianity. I do not know that the time has yet come when anybody needs to apologize for his adherence to the Christian creed; at any rate I do not feel like doing so. I do not think that the Presbyterian body, or the body that is behind-Queen's university, has any reason to apologise for the fact that they have established this educational institution as a Christian institution. The adherents of the Presbyterian church in Canada have, as I said, at great cost and sacrifice to themselves, built up an educational establishment, which, for some reason, they now desire to have declared undenominational. They come to this parliament for legislation, perhaps they should have gone to some other legislative body. I do not know anything about that. However, it seems to me, that if there is to be any transfer of property or of jurisdiction or of authority of any kind, surely the people at whose cost the establishment has been created and maintained, are the people to say under what conditions that transfer of autlfbrity or of jurisdiction shall be made. I say that if the Presbyterian church, having come to this parliament and asked for this legislation, this parliament does not see fit to grant the legislation as asked for, on the terms asked for, -then, let parliament refuse to sanction the proposal, and let the condition remain as it is. But, as an adherent of the Presbyterian church, and having some slight interest in the welfare of that body, and the educational organizations under it, I would certainly protest against this parliament amending the proposal that has come from the owners of that property. The duty of this House is either to accept the proposal

as it is made, or to refuse it, for reasons which should be given. I understand there is some difference of opinion in the Presbyterian church itself as to the advisability of this step, but, it would be absolutely unfair to amend this legislation, without giving the Presbyterian body who applied for it, an opportunity to say whether they would agree to the amendment or not.

I wish to make my position clear on this question. If this university is to continue under the Presbyterian church, I can understand that they might object to any religious denominations having the right to occupy a chair in the university, but if it is going to be undenominational, I do not think they should impose such a restriction as is here suggested. For instance, if a body of Catholics, sold a Catholic church to a body of Presbyterians, the Catholics would not have the right to put in a clause that the Methodists should be excluded from worship in that church. That is the view I take. I do not want to interfere in the domestic matters of the Presbyterian church, but if the Presbyterians are handing over this university as an undenominational institution, I say this par-hament cannot sanction a clause excluding any religious sect.

I quite agree that if the institution is to become national, it certainly should not be in any sense sectarian, but the point I am trying to submit is that assuming the Presbyterian church to be the proprietor of this university, if they wish to have a change of status with respect to it, then let the House accord in the change asked for, or else absolutely refuse, but do not let us amend it so that the Presbyterian church, in dealing with this valuable educational institution, shall be forced by the supreme authority of this parliament, to accept legislation that the Presbyterian church does not want.

I confess that I can not see what my hon. friend (Mr. Bicker-dike) finds in this Bill to insult the Jews. It has often happened that we have found it necessary to incorporate an institution connected with some particular church, and this legislation is going only a little wider and incorporating an institution connected with all the Christian churches of the country. I find on the order paper Bill No. 70, which is entitled ' An Act to Incorporate the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Keewatin,' and in that Bill it is provided that all property, real and personal, churches, schools, colleges and so on, possessed or enjoyed by the Right Rev. D. Charlebois, or the church in communion with the Church of Rome, are declared to be vested in a corporation. Well, there is
no one who would take any objection to that.
That is denominational.

Yes, but it is not an insult to the Jews, although it excludes them, and it is not an insult to the Presbyterians or the Methodists, although it excludes them also. In this Bill, respecting Queen's university, the applicants are applying for legislation that will apply to all Christian churches alike. We are not excluding anybody, but we are providing for the education of people belonging to all the Christian churches of this country, and I do not think there is any ground whatever for saying that that is an insult to anybody. The Jews do not pretend that they have put any of their money in this institution.
I have not heard that the public are going to put any money into it. The money is contributed, by private individuals who are interested in education; and should it not be in the power of these people to say, we want our money devoted to Christian education-not to Jewish, pagan or any other than Christian education? I think that is a fair proposition in a free country like this, and I do not see any good reason for the attitude taken by my hon. friend from Montreal.

Does my hon. friend think that we in parliament have any right to say that because a man has not in the past put money into an institution, he shall not avail himself of it to get an education, be he Jew or Christian?
This does not stop him.

It indirectly stops him by putting a ban upon him, by making him believe that he is going where he is not wanted. I suppose I am as much wedded to the Christian religion as any other man in this House, but I consider that anyone who tries to convert a Jew by depriving him of his state rights is doing a very un-Christian thing. We have no right to put a mark against a Jew, or even an atheist, in this matter. It is not entirely a matter of the Presbyterian church. The Presbyterian church is not able to do what it wants to do without the legislation of this parliament, and it comes here and asks us to approve of what it is doing, and to give it a greater strength than it could have without that legislation; and it wants us to draw a line between the Jew and the Christian as to education. This is a place where we render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. We have no business here to do anything towards the salvation of souls. The man who says that he is in this House for the purpose of doing the work of the churches is mistaken upon the constitution and is very nearly a hypocrite. We have no

business to attempt to affect prejudicially or otherwise the religion or_ non-religion of anyone who is a loyal citizen of King George. Therefore, I cannot vote for this, and I think we ought to be very careful before we establish any such precedent.

The hon. member for Lincoln evidently misapprehends the scope of the measure." The original charter of the university made it distinctly clear that no religious test should be required of any student who entered the walls of Queen's, vested the control of the university in 27 trustees, of whom 12 were to be ministers of the Presbyterian church and 15 laymen in full communion with such church. In 1889 and again in 1906 a widening power was obtained from this parliament, by which the graduates and the members of the council obtained the right of electing ten members to the board of trustees. The attitude of the church at the present moment is as follows :	They say that the Presbyterian
church through our 27 trustees have control of the university and of its funds. The church says tve raised $800,000 as an endowment of that university, and we are quite willing to turn it over to the board of trustees of the university to be elected by the benefactors and! the graduates. We desire that those who are going to fill the professors' chairs shall be men who profess Christianity. As I have explained to the House, I do not agree with the Presbyterian church or that branch of it which contends for this provision; but I do agree with the contention that t'he Presbyterian church, in handing over $800,000 and a university has a right to say into what hands that work shall be entrusted. I do not think it ever crossed the mind of the Presbyterian church or the representatives of the university that this would give offence to the Jews. If I catch correctly the spirit of the Presbyterian church, this was aimed not at the Jew, but at the agnostic and the atheist, because the Presbyterian church desires to maintain this great educational institution Christian, require those set to educate the youth of Canada to be Christians, to believe in the divinity of Christ. It is ridiculous to construe this as an insult to the Jews or to any other class of people. If the Jews came to-morrow and desired to incorporate a university confined to the adherents of their faith, I would vote for it as readily as I do for this Bill, recognizing as I do the right of all religious sects to educate their people in the faith of their fathers. The hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) will see that the word ' non-denominational ' is used. That word is not us broad as * non-sectarian.' ' Nondenominational ' includes the branches of Mr. LANCASTER.
the Christian churches. ' Non-sectarian ' would be inconsistent, with the purpose of the Bill. Under the Bill, all branches of the Christian church are welcomed to its board, and to its professors' chairs, but only those who profess Christianity shall be entitled to occupy those positions; and, as the ex-Minister of the Interior says, why should not the Presbyterian church be allowed to give this great gift to the nation, and to widen the sphere of its influence?
Does the hon. gentleman say that we are justified in being sectarian and not in being denominational?

I think it is within the sphere of parliament, so far as the objects are good, to incorporate any body of men to carry out a benevolent or charitable purpose, and in the carrying out of that work, it has a right to say that the members of the board of management shall be members of their own faith. That is the principle on which this legislation is founded. It is non-sectarian, it offers no insult to any person, but it says you cannot take advantage of our gifts unless you are members of our faith. I say that it is consistent on the part of the Presbyterian church, although I do not agree with the premises from which they reason.

My hon. friend the ex-Minister of the Interior stood up very strongly for the Presbyterian church, and I was very pleased to see him get so religious all of a sudden.
Now my hon. friend from Guysborough said it was really Christianity versus something else. In my opinion that is not a correct statement. The other denominations are opposing this legislation as well as the Jews.
What denominations?

The Baptists are opposing it. Let me read what the official organ of the Baptists says about this Bill. I am about to quote from the 'Canadian Baptist,' which is the mouthpiece of the Baptish Church of Canada. The article says:
There was passed, without amendment, by the Private Bills Committee of the House of Commons at Ottawa, on Friday last, the Queen's College Bill, and it will now come before the House itself. Before the Private Bills Committee, a strenuous protest was made by certain Hebrew bodies, who feel that the Bill as proposed shuts them out from privileges which should be theirs as citizens of the Dominion of Canada.
I would like my hon. friend the exMinister of the Interior to remember that the Jews are citizens of Canada, that

On section 1,
Will the hon. gentleman please explain?

The general tenor of this clause is to deal with the classifications in the post office outside service. It dispenses with senior and junior, and created classes with Grade A and B. It does away with the class known as stampers and sorters; with what was known as the fourth class and also with the junior third class. The stampers and sorters, the fourth -class, and the junior third class, become third class. Grade B stampers and sorters under the existing law receive $500 and go up to $600 with increments of $50 a year. The fourth class commences with $500 and goes to $700 with increases of $100 a year; the junior third class goes from $700 to $800. All these are replaced by third class Grade B, and the officers in this class will receive $500 on appointment, and will go to $800 with annual increases

of $100. What is now the senior third class and the junior second will become third class Grade A. At present a senior third class clerk receives from $800 to $900, increasing by $50 a year, and the junior second commences s,t $900 and goes to $1,000 by two increases of $50 a year each. These two become third class Grade B with a salary of $800 to begin at and the maximum will be $1,000 by increases of $50 per annum. Senior second class clerks now receive $1,000 per year and they will in future have $1,200 as a maximum. It is divided into two grades: second class Grade B, the salary of which begins at $1,000 and goes to $1,200, and second class Grade A, the salary of which begins at $1,200 and goes to $1,400, which is $200 more than the present maximum of the second class. The first class, which at present ranges in salary from $1,200 to $1,500, and in which there was no junior or senior grade, will be subdivided into two grades: one, class Grade B beginning at $1,400 and going to $1,600, and the other class Grade A, beginning at $1,600 and going to $1,800; an increase of $200 on the minimum and $300 on the present maximum. This Bill introduces a class called chief clerks in post offices with an annual revenue of $500,000 or over, and there will be one chief clerk for every two hundred employees.
This will for the moment apply solelv to the three largest post offices-Toronto, Montreal -and Winnipeg. The salary of the chief clerk will begin at $1,800 and go to $2,200. The salary of the superintendent will begin at $1,800, the present salary, and will go up to $2,500. This is the general purport of the Bill. Most of these clauses were in the Bi'll which was presented to the House last year by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), but which was prevented from passing by the arrival of the Sergeant-at-Arms at the door; therefore, I suppose my hon. friend will concur with me in finding this a good measure.

On general lines I commend this legislation. The Bill is similar to the one which was introduced last year, and which was on the eve of receiving consideration from this House, but was unfortunately prevented from passing on account of the visit of the Black Bod. The increases and changes- which are made are certainly most desirable. I can only emphasize the fact that the time has come I believe, when we should dispense with all this phraseology, and as far as possible bring the outside service under the Civil Service Act. In fact, the Bill of last year was prepared with that end in view, and I suppose the amounts mentioned in this Bill have reference to the classification which w-e find in the inside service, so that Mr. PELLETIER.
when the change takes place and the outside service is brought under the Commission, there will be no difficulty in classifying the various offices.

I desire to read a letter I have received.
In looking over Bill No. 106 that has been introduced in the House of Commons, I find that so far as second-class clerks in the post office are concerned, it contains a very unfair discrimination. Frequent representations have been made, as you know, for a general increase in the salaries of post office clerks without the least suggestion of political discrimination. But the Bill that has -been introduced makes discrimination in favour of those who were appointed by Conservative governments.
In referring to the second-class clerks, page 3, line 25, you will see that those who have had less than 15 years service, temporary or permanent, are placed in grade B; again at line 32 on the same page, any one who has had fifteen years' service or over, whether temporary or permanent, goes into grade A. This practically means that there will be no increase in salary for second-class clerks appointed during the Liberal term of office. While the Bill does not say that these differ-erences shall date -from July of 1896, by putting the period at twelve years, it practically and very effectively gives the preference to those who were appointed by a Conservative government as against those who have been appointed since. I am satisfied that a question in the House as to the number of persons that were affected as appointees before and after the fifteen years' limit with the dates of their appointment, would show the large

preponderance of Conservatives whom this Act will beneficially affect.
I am told that employees who were letter carriers from Conservative appointment prior to 1896 were in many cases advanced to clerkships with a large increase in salary. This Bill would displace clerks at present (from seniors by reason of the efficient discharge of their duties) who have not had fifteen years' service, but who held clerkships before the others reached that rank in the service. In addition to the matter to which I refer, it is suggested that the fair application of the benefits of the Bill to all parties will be obtained by striking out in line 28, page 3 the following words: ' and he was a senior second-class prior to the 1st day of October, 1909 "; and in the 33rd line by striking ont the words 1 temporary and permanent " and substituting the words ' in that case.'
