Mr. THOMSON (Qu'Appelle) I wish to move:
That the Bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred baok to the Committee of the Whole for the purpose of amendment by striking out subsection 2 of seotion 57 and substituting therefore the following :
Notwithstanding any provisions in this Aot that may conflict therewith, sample markets may be established under such rules and regulations as shall be recommended by the board and approved by the Governor in Council, in the city of Winnipeg, and such other point or points as shall be selected by the board with the approval of the Governor in Council.
The. change which would be effected by this amendment, if adopted, would be in the first place, that instead of as at present providing for three points for sample markets-that is Winnipeg, Fort William and Calgary-a market would be established at Winnipeg and such other point or points as shall be selected by the board, with the approval of the Governor in Council. At present, 1 believe, the only place at which people generally appear to have asked for a sample market is Winnipeg. There is no objection, to a sample market being established there, but I think it would be necessary to have sample markets at other points. I do not think it is well to limit the places at which these markets may be established. They may be necessary at Calgary and Fort William, but they are just as likely to be necessary at other points. This is a matter which might well be left in the hands of the board with the approval of the Governor in Council, because circumstances may arise which might make it advisable to establish sample markets at other points. For instance, a considerable quantity of grain is being shipped to the United States. The grain from the western part of Saskatchewan, and parts of Alberta is being shipped to that country, and it will go over the Soo line. Therefore, it would be advisable to have a sample market at Moosejaw or North Portal or some such place. This amendment will leave the board free to select such points as they may deem advisable. My chief reason for moving this amendment is because of the provision which permits the mixing of grain. There are two or three things that seem to the farmers of the west to Be very important in connection with the grain trade. One of these has been dealt with in connection with car distribution. Another equally im-

portant question is that of the mixing of grain. The western farmers rightly or wrongly, and I believe rightly, deem it to be very important to them that mixing should not be allowed.^ I do not think they would seriously object to mixing provided all terminal elevators were operated by the government. But we must remember that we have not any positive promise from the Minister of Trade and Commerce that such a policy will be carried out. He merely says that he proposes to try the experiment with one or two elevators, or possibly more, and there is no reason to suppose government control of terminal elevators generally will be carried out. On that account, the western farmers are utterly dissatisfied with the provision to which I have referred. I fear the Minister looks on the grain growers as spoiled^ children who have had too much of their* own way in the past. It is true that a great many amendments have been made to the Manitoba Grain Act at their request since it was first put in force, but I think if the Minister of Trade and Commerce will look into the recommendations of the western grain growers asking for amendment to that Act, he will find that they have been for the benefit of the country at large, and not merely in the interest of the grain growers themselves. Everybody must recognize that the great growth of Canada in late years, has been caused by the development of the west and the increase in the amount of grain which has been grown and exported from that country. To allow mixing to take place is bound to be one of the most serious blows that can be struck at the western farmer. .

In seconding the amendment, I merely wish to state that the amendment is in the interest of the grain crowers of the west to a large extent. Since this Bill first came before the House I in common with other members, have received a great many communications dealing with this Bill in its various stages, and among the clauses which have received the condemnation of the grain growers as a whole, is the one which allows the mixing of grain in terminal elevators. That section has caused a great deal of dissatisfaction among grain growers. In my judgment the clause has been inserted largely for the benefit of the grain dealers, as against the interest of the grain growers. The object of the latter in past years has been to prevent the bad practice of mixing, which has prevailed at the terminal elevators. If these elevators were owned and operated by the government, I believe this evil might be controlled to a very large extent, but under the provisions of the Bill only one or two such elevators are going to be run by the government. Consequently the farmers view with a great

deal of alarm the fact that other elevators which are privately owned, may continue to go on mixing the grain in the same nefarious manner in which it has been done in the past, which practice it has been the object of the Manitoba Grain Act to overcome in every possible way. For these reasons I very gladly second the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle.

I do not want hon. gentlemen opposite to think that because I did not answer the arguments of the gentlemen who moved and seconded the former amendment that I treated that amendment otherwise than it should have been treated. I did not make any answer because the arguments advanced, so far as I can judge, were practicaly the arguments that had been already adduced, and that were thoroughly threshed out as we went through committee, and I did not consider it necessary to take up the time of the House in repeating arguments in rebuttal. The same thing applies to the present amendment, and yet I think it is well for me to take a moment or two in dealing with this amendment especially. There is not, I think, very much difference between the mover of this amendment and myself as the sponsor for the Bill. He argues, and wishes to make effective, that the selection of sample markets shall be left with the Board of Commissioners and subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. The Bill states three principal places at which sample markets, not necessarily shall, but may be established. It does not seem to me that sample markets in the west, or anywhere else, are, like the measles and smal'l-pox, breaking out at unexpected moments.
We meet here every year and we have a chance to legislate each year, and I think that no interest will suffer in the interim between sessions, and no sudden and unexpected development is likely to take place which would mark out a certain place -which had not been provided for in the Act as a necessary place for a sample market. I think we should go gradually in fixing sample market places in the west and that the growth should not be over rapid. When you make your provision for Calgary for a sample market, for instance, that does not say that it will be a sample market this year, or next year, or the year after. This Bill, when it becomes law, does not establish a sample market anywhere, but simply makes it possible for a sample market to be established at that place; but the co-operation of other factors than the government and other conditions than those for which the government can be responsible, are necessary before a sample market can be established. Now, as the spot upon which

we are all agreed for a sample market if there is one at all, we take Winnipeg. There is no cavil about that. I think that it has been demonstrated that Fort William is another place where a fairly good sample market could be established. It is unique in its position at the head of lake navigation and in connection with the rail transport of grain; and, with the press of cars from Winnipeg and the time that elapses between their being sampled and graded at Winnipeg and their arrival at Fort William, there are conditions that may arise that will make Fort William a good place for a sample market. It is not improbable, also, that Fort William will become a large milling centre in the course of time. It has a good location in that respect. For these reasons it is a likely place for a sample market. The same is true of Calgary, far remote from these other two. If it ever does become a sample market, it will be because of the western export of the grain by the Pacific ocean. That may develop pretty rapidly. I would not take the responsibility of saying that we should not make provision this year for Calgary as a point for a sample market, because, with the great production of grain and the necessary congestion which is physically unmovable towards the east, it is not out of probability that next year may see a very large efflux of grain from the prairie provinces, especially from Alberta and part of Saskatchewan, towards the Pacific ocean; if not next year, then certainly the year after.
So that, I think, we have covered all the present possible points for a successful sample market in the three places we have named in the Act. If, when we come here next year, it is found that Edmonton, or Prince Rupert, or Moosejaw, or some other place has developed towards the point where successful markets can be established, we can make provision therefor. But I think we shall all agree that to endeavour to have a large number of small sample markets, would be rather against having a successful sample market at all. The success of the sample market depends on the large number of buyers and the large aggregation of sellers, coming together in a certain place, together with other conditions which Winnipeg and Fort William at present, and Calgary in the near future, pretty well fulfil. So, I do not think there is much difference in fact and in reality between my hon, friend (Mr. Thomson, Qu'Appelle) and my-self.
Now, with reference to mixing: What is it that the farmers dreaded and dread to day, in mixing? I have had the pleasure of reading about it in the Grain Growers' Guide-and I read that journal very regularly, and have appreciated much that it
contains, though I do not agree with everything it says. It is not for me to offer advice to the grain growers on the conduct of their paper; but if I were running a paper in the west, on agricultural lines, I would try to be more hopeful, I would try to inculcate through the columns of the paper some friendly advice, some kindly suggestion, some enumeration of the advantages of the country, some suggestions of the better and newer methods. I would not paint the whole situation black; I would have a reasonable portion of clear and lively colour. But I am not running the ' Grain Growers' Guide.' The grain growers who run the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' put one leg upon the mixing and another leg upon the government-owned elevators, and they say: Mixing is horrible, but we are willing to embrace it if we have only honest conduct of the elevators.	Well, honest conduct of the elevators is what this government is going to see is carried out. It is going to do it by the added machinery, which this Bill is to put into their hands. It is going to do it by the nomination of a first-class grain commission which has no interested sympathy with elevator companies or with railroad corporations, but which has first and mainly the farmers' interest in view and will use both elevators and railway companies as very helpful means to aid the farmers in quick and proper despatch of their grain to the markets of the world. Now, I defy any one to read the discussion in the Grain Growers' Guide upon the sample market without coming to the conclusion that if there is not a preponderance of sentiment in favour of the sample market with mixing, there is at least a fairly even division of opinion. I would invite my hon. friend to read the last, or the next to the last, number of the Grain Growers' Guide and the resolutions and discussions upon these resolutions, and he, will see that they are in favour of a sample market absolutely, provided they have honest conduct of the elevators at the terminal points. These gentlemen want,-they ask for, and have a right to ask for,-a certain thing, and the government is in duty bound to give what they ask for. But, the government and the House have a perfect right to use .its judgment as to how that thing shall be brought about. Mr. Fream and Mr. McKenzie say it cannot be brought about except by government-owned elevators. The government believe that with the machinery that is provided in this Bill, they can bring it about; and I am willing to stake my reputation and the reputation of the government on the fact that it will be brought about in the administration of this Act during this and the succeeding years. If they get the thing they want, honest mixing with a sample market, what

is the trouble that they need fear. I do not find fault with the farmers in the west for fearing. But that which they fear is based upon suspicion and not upon actual facts. ' Once bitten, twice shy.' The farmers in olden times were bitten, bitten by the elevator men and bitten by the railroad men. But the legislation of 1905-6 revolutionized the matter of transportation of grain in that country. This Act and the administration of this Act, and the government behind this Act, does not mean to take away one iota of the privileges which the farmers of the west have for the proper disposal of their grain. If they can help them in any way they will do it. Why should I, or why should the government, collude with the elevator men or with the railroad men as against the farmers of the west ?
The whole argument of my hon. friends opposite sink to the ground, disappear utterly, unless you can prove that there would be collusion between three parties; the elevator men, the railway men and the grain commission. Now, I do not believe that the grain commission is going to collude with either the elevator men or the railroad men to the detriment of the farmers; it is going to aid both the elevators and the railroad companies, and I believe, with their consent and with their co-operation, to do everything that possibly can be done for the speedy marketing of the farmers' grain. Now, I would not ask that this Bill be passed if I thought it was going to do what Mr. Fream fears it will do. He says: You had better knock the Bill out entirely rather than have these going to have that effect I would be just added clauses in it. If I thought it was as much against that clause as Mr. Fream or Mr. McKenzie. We all have a right to cur opinions. I do not judge any one as not being honest and straight in the opinion he holds of what might take place. But it cannot be a well based opinion yet, it is nothing more than a fear or a suspicion; and I think he will find that the fear is groundless, and that the suspicion will not eventuate in fact.

I must congratulate my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) on having succeeded in waking up the minister at last. During the last day or so that we have been dealing with this Bill the minister has either ignored our criticisms, or given them scant courtesy. He has entered into a more or less general discussion of the matter, defending the commission that is going to be appointed. Now he has one great advantage over us, he has some sort of an idea whom he is going to appoint on the commission, whereas we do not know at all what men the government have in their minds. Nor do we know, when they come to bring down sup-Mir. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
plementary estimates, how much money they will ask parliament to vote for the purpose of securing the control and operation of government elevators at the head of the lakes. . The minister's whole _ argument is that he would not ask parliament to put this measure through if he did not believe it was a good one. He speaks of ' My commission' and says it is going to be so immaculate and perfect that it should have the confidence of every member of this committee, as if we ought to vote without hesitation any legislation the minister proposes. For my part I do not propose to accept any legislation merely because the minister asks us to do so. We might just as well go home if we are going to vote for a certain piece of legislation just because the minister says he would not present it to the House if his motives were not good in proposing it. I think the minister will see that while we are not reflecting upon his bona fides in the_ matter, he cannot bring us to the conviction by simply saying that he would not do it if he did not think he was perfectly right. But he has gone beyond the mere amendment in your hands, and has spoken about the Bill being so satisfactory, and when it is passed there are going to be such safeguards surrounding the handling of grain at the head of the lakes, and such a fine commission to handle it, that he has no doubt at all everything will be satisfactory to the farmers. It is a remarkable thing that when this Bill was before the House last May, hon. gentlemen opposite declared they could not support it because it did not suit them, and now we find them throwing up their hats in support of a Bill of the very same tenor.

I would1 remind the hon.
gentleman that, under a similar ruling, it is scarcely permissible to refer to anything that is not before the House. I do not think it would be wise to wander far away from the present amendment.

When I rose to my feet I proposed to speak particularly on that part of my hon. friend's amendment, and to his suggestion that the minister might take to the board power to establish sample markets at any place that the government or the board might deem proper. I think 'that is a suggestion the minister might take into consideration, even at this late hour. I speak of this more particularly from' the view point of the town I have the honour to represent. From the city of Moosejaw there have gone south this year, into the American market, car load1 after car load, train load after train load, of wheat, after paying the duty. I have seen reports from the Minneapolis, St. Pau' and Sault Ste. Marie railroad saying that their traffic was congested with wheat from the Canadian west. That is an illustration of

what may occur which would make it de-! sirable that the government should have in its hands power to adjust the administration of this Act according to changing circumstances from time to time. There have gone from the city of Moosejaw possibly millions of bushels of wheat, going down south by the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie railway, which leaves the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway at Moosejaw. Another year some other set of circumstances might arise. We have been told during the late election campaign that we should not encourage reciprocity, because the Americans would take off the duty anyway. Let us suppose that they did remove their duty from our cereals and admit the product of our soil free of duty, there would be such a demand from the United States that our cereals would go south in immense quantities. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the American people prefer to purchase in a .sample market. Practically all their buying is done in Minnesota and other places by sample in a sample market, and if a sample market would be popular for any purchasers it would be with American purchasers. Therefore I suggest that the minister should take to himself power in this Act to establish sample markets wherever the government and the board might think it well to do so. More than that, one of the important customers of the sample market is the mill. We know that the great mills of Minneapolis are the greatest customers of the sample market in Minnesota. In the city of Moosejaw there is a greater demand for wheat for milling purposes than there is in the city of Calgary; there are more milling facilities in the city of Moosejaw than in the city of Calgary. Therefore, I say there is a much stronger reason for making Moosejaw a sample market than Calgary. I do not propose that the name of Moosejaw be put in the Bill, but I propose that the minister take power to establish as many sample markets as circumstances may render desirable.

In proposing this amendment, I do so for the purpose of placing before the House in this formal way, the same issue which I placed before the Committee of the Whole some two weeks agp. My contention is that the Bill as proposed by the government has absolutely no meaning, and is absolutely ineffective. This Bill, more or less makes a pretense of forbidding men who operate terminal elevators, from, at the same time, buying and selling grain, but, when it comes to be studied, it makes only a pretense of that because it does not in any way effectively attain that result. It distinctly says that any person who manages a leased elevator, where the lease is approved by the board, may buy or sell grain. I need not go further into the question than to show that that one feature of it makes the section absolutely useless. If a person wishes to be put in possession of an elevator and to have control, of the management

and operation of it, all he has to do is to become a lessee of it or to become a member of a company which is a lessee of it, or be in any way associated with the leasing of such an elevator, and then he may buy and sell grain to his heart's content. I submit that once the Minister of Trade and Commerce grants that, and he cannot deny it, he must agree with me that the whole clause is absolutely useless. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in reply to a question I put him this afternoon, assured me that the farmers were safe in the hands of the government. That is a fragile basis to put this legislation on. The farmers do not hold that view. The Minister of Trade and Commerce implied, although he did not say it, that the representations that have been read in this chamber coming from the Association of Grain Growers, and coming from the secretaries of the different provincial associations which group together the district associations; that they did not represent the people in any fuli measure. The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not use these words, but he made the remark that there was a great part of the farming community that was not making its voice heard when we spoke, and when we read these resolutions that we have read in the House from time to time. I read to him, and I will place it again on ' Hansard a telegram I received this morning from Mr. Fred. W. Greene, secretary of the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, a gentleman holding the very responsible position of secretary for a group of all the Grain Growers' Associations of the greatest grain growing province in the Dominion. If you could concentrate in the expression of one man anything that is worthy of attention, I say the attention of the House and of the minister should be given to a communication from the Secretary of the Grain Growers' Association in the great wheat province of Saskatchewan. This is what he says:
Farmers are fearful that through the influence of elevator and transportation companies at Ottawa, farmers' friends will be handicapped and their interests sacrificed. Our association is ready to send delegation if in vour opinion their cause may he assisted.

I was in hopes there might be time given to these men to come down here and state their case, and they can state it better than any of us in this House can state it, try as we may and repeat ais we may at times, our arguments to the wearying of the minister and of hon. gentlemen opposite, a great many of whom do not belong to the west and do not understand details. And until recently hon. members on the other side, including the Prime Minister, believed in the same thing. Let me read a resolution brought down on the 13th of February last by the ho.n. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) bearing out this idea. I have already said that we had been trying to solve problems connected with the line elevators. Government ownership would dispose of that question which is a most important one, and I think the greatest danger in this Bill is the provision with regard to the distribution of cars. I have received a number of letters and resolutions from different portions of my riding none of them favouring such provisions as are in the Bill giving the board discretionary powers; they are all opposed to it. I think the farmers of the west believed that this question had been settled some years ago, and now they will be surprised to find that this parliament has practically revoked the protection which they formerly had and has given a discretion which may be very much abused by the board. I have letters from grain growers' associations in my riding at Hanley, Elbow, Aber deen, War man, Hawarden, Haleyonia, Ardath >and Floral. I believe they represent the .sentiments of the grain growers, and it would be their wish, as it is my judgment, that this Bill should be defeated rather than put into force, and that they rely on the provision of the Manitoba Grain Act as it now stands.

One thing occurs to me in connection with the matter. For the last two or three years, in the House of Commons and throughout western Canada we were promised by the Conservative party government ownership and operation of terminal elevators, and were also promised the control of our natural resources if the Conservative party got into power. In fact the only thing that saved the Conservative party in Saskatchewan and Alberta from complete extinction was the promise made to the electors of government ownership and the return of the natural resources to these provinces. The government has had an opportunity to restore the natural resources to one province, but they have not fulfilled this promise. They had an opportunity to-day when dealing with the Grain Act to give us government ownership and operation of terminal elevators, but we have now in this Bill absolutely nothing more than was in Bill (Q) of the Senate, which was before

the House of Commons in 1910-11. When I look at the hon. members from Manitoba, the member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), the member for Souris (Mr. SchafEner), the member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe)-I do not think the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) committed himself to government ownership and operation of terminal elevators-and read their speeches of last year I begin to wonder if they are the same men who were here last session. The hon. member for Souris said this was absolutely the only remedy. The hon. members for Selkirk and Lisgar said the same thine, yet what do we find to-day, every one of these gentlemen is supporting practically every clause of the Bill as brought forward by the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) and not one provision beyond what was contained in Bill (Q) of last year, in favour of government ownership. How do they reconcile their position of to-day with that of the last few years?

It is a most serious matter to move against the passage of a Bill which is an amendment to an Act that has been on the statute-book for a number of years, an Act which relates to the operation of the grain trade, which grain trade amounts to tens of millions of dollars a year, and the increase of which trade is the true foundation of Canada's wealth and prosperity ait the present time, and its absolute hope for the future. When the Bill was first submitted to the House this session, it was practically the Bill that was passed by the Senate and brought down to this House last session.
That Bill as it came before the House embodied a certain principle. That principle was the protection given by legislative authority to the rights and interests of the grain producer. It is because that principle of the Bill has been reversed by the amendments which have been made to

I listened with great attention to the lecture or sermon that was preached by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the second reading of the Bill, or when it went into committee, when he told us of the desire which filled his bosom to have all classes of people who were interested in grain view each other's transactions with confidence, his idea being to promote harmony amongst all the different interests. Are they going to protect the interest of the producer or the interest of the dealer in the product? My hon. friend, by the amendments which he has introduced to this Bill} in committee, has established the fact that from this' time forward this Grain Act is to be in the interest of the grain dealer and in the interest of the grain transporter, and not in the interest of the grain producer. They have with great labour and pains, with the assistance of their representatives on both sides of the House, been successful in building up an Act which to them was satisfactory in large measure. Therefore, the producers of grain in the west were asking from time to time for further amendments of the Grain Act and for further and further consideration of their interests, always believing that the mind of parliament on both sides was to give them adequate protection. >But in the process of .this Bill passing through committee, without due warning at the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the principle of the Bill has been reversed, and to-day the Bill,

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is the duty of the Speaker to inquire if an hon. member heard the question put. It is for the hon. member to say ' yes ' or ' no '. If he says ' yes ', he has the right to vote.
May I inquire if the vote of the hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) is to be counted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I understood the hon. member correctly, he said he was within the precincts of the House and heard the question put.
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Did the hon. member for North Lanark hear the question put?

Yes sir.
Motion agreed to and Bill read a third time and passed.
Mr. BORDEN moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will take any of the Bills and resolutions on the order paper that are ready and then Supply.
Will the Manitoba Boundary Bill come up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I believe that is first for consideration to-morrow and then we will go on with the other Bills and afterwards Supply.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.40 a. m., Tuesday.
Tuesday, March 12, 1912.
